v.q: Which are the four pillars of object-oriented programming?
o: Encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance and polymorphism
Compilation, linking, loading and execution
Class, object, method and variable
Public, private, protected and static
v.w: Most interviews expect a short definition plus a quick example for each of the four.

v.q: Which is NOT one of the four pillars of object-oriented programming?
o: Compilation
Encapsulation
Inheritance
Polymorphism
v.w: The pillars are encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance and polymorphism.

v.q: What does encapsulation mean in practice?
o: Keep state private and expose behaviour through an interface
Make every field public for easy access
Put every class together in a single file
Copy objects instead of ever sharing them
v.w: Callers cannot put the object in an invalid state, and the internals can change without breaking them.

v.q: Which class design shows good encapsulation?
o: Private fields, checked setters
Public fields anyone can set
Static fields used by everyone
One giant method doing it all
v.w: Hiding state lets the class enforce rules, such as a balance never going negative.

o: One call behaves differently depending on the actual object type
A class that has been declared with a great many fields
Methods that are able to return several values at once
A class that gets compiled several times in a build
v.w: Runtime (overriding) polymorphism lets code depend on an interface such as `PaymentMethod` while each implementation behaves its own way.

v.q: Which call is resolved at run time by polymorphism?
o: An overridden instance method
A static method call
A call to a private method
A call to a final method
v.w: The JVM picks the overriding method of the actual object. Static, private and final calls are fixed earlier.

v.q: What is the difference between overloading and overriding?
o: Overloading: same name, new parameters. Overriding: a subclass replaces a method
Overloading is decided at run time, overriding at compile time
Overloading means changing only the return type of a method
They are simply two different names for the same mechanism
v.w: Overloads are chosen at compile time from the argument types. Overrides are chosen at run time from the object's real class.

v.q: Which statement about overloading is NOT true?
o: It is chosen at run time by the object type
The parameter lists differ
It is chosen at compile time
Return type alone cannot distinguish it
v.w: Overloads are resolved at compile time from the declared argument types. Overriding is resolved at run time.

v.q: When should you prefer composition over inheritance?
o: You reuse behaviour without a rigid is-a hierarchy
Only when the class has no methods at all
Whenever a class needs to hold fields
Never, because inheritance is always better
v.w: Inheritance couples subclass to superclass internals. Composition allows swapping parts at runtime and is easier to test.

v.q: Which situation favours composition over inheritance?
o: A car has an engine
A circle is a shape
A savings account is an account
A manager is an employee
v.w: A has-a relationship is modelled by a field, and the part can be swapped without changing the hierarchy.

v.q: What is the difference between an abstract class and an interface in Java?
o: A class can implement many interfaces but extend one abstract class that may hold state
Interfaces can hold instance fields, while abstract classes cannot hold any
Abstract classes are not allowed to contain implemented methods
Interfaces can be instantiated directly with the `new` keyword
v.w: Since Java 8 interfaces can have default methods, but still no instance state. Use an abstract class to share state and code.

v.q: Which statement about interfaces and abstract classes is NOT true?
o: A class can extend several abstract classes
A class can implement several interfaces
An abstract class can hold state
An interface cannot be instantiated
v.w: Java allows only one superclass but many interfaces.

v.q: A `Square` extends `Rectangle` but breaks code that sets width and height separately. Which principle is violated?
o: Liskov substitution: a subtype must work wherever its base type does
Open-closed: classes should be closed to extension
Single responsibility: one reason to change
Interface segregation: keep interfaces small
v.w: If substituting the subtype changes expected behaviour, the inheritance hierarchy is wrong.

v.q: Which rule says a subclass must be usable wherever its parent is expected?
o: Liskov substitution
Single responsibility
Open-closed
Dependency inversion
v.w: If code breaks with the subtype, the inheritance is wrong, like a Square that is not a real Rectangle.

o: Exposing what an object does while hiding how it does it
Splitting a single class across many different source files
Declaring every method of a class as static for speed
Removing code from the project once it is no longer used
v.w: Callers use `Repository.save(x)` without knowing whether it writes to SQL, a file or memory.

o: List, hiding how items are stored
A public int[] field
A giant main method
A hard-coded class name
v.w: Callers use what the type does and do not depend on its internals.
